brief: JPMorgan's Dubravko Lakos-Bujas frames 2026's AI-buildout bottleneck as moving from chips to funding and now, after the midterms, to regulation. A national data-center moratorium stays unlikely (Senate's 60-vote threshold, presidential veto, Trump's support), so the binding constraint shifted to states: Texas (immediate moratorium), Georgia and New Mexico (project pauses), Ohio and Nevada (utility-cost conditions), plus 42 of 45 local ballot measures passing or leaning that way. JPM says 2027 hyperscaler capex stays "relatively insulated" at $1.7 trillion versus $1.3 trillion consensus, floored near $1.5 trillion. Every $100 billion of capex adds about $9 of S&P EPS, so even the floor adds 4-5% to 2027 index earnings. The curve, which JPM has rising 87% in 2027 then 19% in 2028, "will likely flatten ahead of 2028" as permitting tightens, with the stated risk being delays, not cancellations. Texas holds 27% of data-center capacity funded in high-yield project finance, so a delay that helps free cash flow could still push leverage higher if monetization slips, as already happened when banks shelved Anthropic's $15 billion Texas junk-bond sale. Markets moved first: JPM's AI/data-center basket fell 13.5% in two sessions while its defensive "Blue Wave" basket outperformed.
